blocks.text: Daniel 12 concludes the vision-oriented half of the book (chapters 7–12), in contrast to the court tales in chapters 1–6. Its promises of deliverance, awakening from the dust, differing lasting destinies, and the shining of the wise make it a major resurrection passage. Yet important questions remain open: “many” need not settle every question about the scope of resurrection, and the passage itself calls for care when relating its imagery to later teachings.

The reference to the removal of the continual offering and the “abomination that maketh desolate” has a horizon in an Antiochene desecration of the temple, while later Jewish and Christian readers have reused the language. Those settings should be distinguished rather than treated as one undifferentiated prediction. Likewise, the chapter’s numbered periods—1,290 and 1,335 days—express revised hope amid crisis, not a basis for confident modern countdowns.

Apocalyptic hope can resist imperial power, but this kind of reading requires safeguards. Interpretations that intensify conspiracy, end-times fear, authoritarian control, nationalism, war, or genocide run contrary to responsible pastoral practice.
